BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Forecast guidance becomes increasingly messy by the weekend, with several solutions favoring active and unsettled weather with lingering precipitation.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Light valley rain and mountain snow expected through Monday afternoon.
- A generally unsettled and wet pattern will continue through next week, with brief dry periods.
- Late week unsettled weather will come alongside warmer temps, with uncertainty on position and inversion development.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A closed low pressure system off of the Pacific Northwest coast will eject a shortwave trough through the region today, with valley rain showers and high terrain snow showers increasing into southwest Idaho this morning. Light snow is falling across southeast Oregon, with light rain expected to move into the Treasure Valley before sunrise. An associated frontal passage will slowly move through the region late Sunday into Monday, with terrain driven showers continuing over the central ID mountains on Monday. Minimal accumulations of both snow and rain are expected with this system, with mountain snowfall amounts between 1 and 3 inches for most locations. High terrain above 7500 ft MSL in the Wallowa Mountains and in the central ID mountains will approach between 4 and 8 inches of storm total snow. Temperatures will generally be near normal, with valleys seeing breezy southeast winds tonight keeping low temperatures above freezing. After the frontal passage, temperatures tomorrow night will lower to near freezing for valley locations. Therefore, Monday morning will see the better potential for a brief rain-snow mix in the Treasure Valley with any lingering showers.

Ridging will build back in late Monday and Tuesday, with generally dry conditions. An inversion will likely develop on Tuesday and Wednesday with low mixing heights across the region, but breezy southeasterly winds and a generally unsettled pattern returning late Wednesday will likely keep impacts from fog and stratus limited.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A potent upper level trough will then move onshore on Wednesday, rapidly weakening by the time it reaches eastern Oregon. Models disagree on extent of precipitation, but light valley rain and high elevation mountain snow will likely come to southeast Oregon and high terrain in southwest Idaho by Wednesday night. Snow levels look to rise to near 5500-6500 feet, although snow cover and lingering cold pools in high terrain valleys will allow for pockets of lower snow levels. Another upper level trough extending down along the western Canada/US coast from a Gulf of Alaska low will likely dampen the amplitude of high pressure over the region on Thursday. This will bring zonal flow over the region and advect moisture with a warm front into the northern tier of the area. The greatest uncertainty with this system lies in primarily the magnitude and extent of the precipitation on Thursday. Cluster guidance favors high pressure pushing the best precipitation chances northward on Friday, with the mountains in northeast Oregon and central Idaho seeing the highest precipitation chances. If this high pressure effectively keeps most of the moisture and zonal flow to the north, as modeled by the AI-GFS deterministic solution, inversion concerns with low stratus and fog in the Snake River Valley could return by late week. This warmer air would also elevate snow levels to near 6500-7500 ft MSL, especially in the Snake River Valley and near the NV border.

Forecast guidance becomes increasingly messy by the weekend, with several solutions favoring active and unsettled weather with lingering precipitation. All model solutions depict some form of another upper level trough or closed low by Sunday, with widely varying storm tracks and impacts for the region. Current forecast favors a 30-50% chance of precipitation for lower elevations, with better confidence for high terrain in Idaho with a 50-70% chance of measurable precipitation.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Upper-level ridging will rebuild across the Rockies behind Monday's disturbance. Afternoon temperatures will gradually warm each day through the week, with mild and dry conditions looking likely for Thursday's holiday celebrations.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Patchy fog through mid-morning for portions of the plains today.
- Another system brings the chance for light mountain snow showers late Monday into Tuesday morning.
- Cooler fall temperatures to continue through mid next week.
- No major travel impacts are expected during the Thanksgiving travel period.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: The Dense Fog Advisory has been canceled. Patchy dense fog remains on the table for portions of the plains through mid-morning, but visibilities below 1/4 mile are not expected to be prolonged nor widespread enough to warrant a broader highlight.
UPDATE Issued at 424 AM MST Sun Nov 22 2026

Stratus has been slow to develop this morning over the plains, with bases also sufficiently high (for now) to limit visibility reductions. Some additional lowering and westward spread is still expected, however it seems increasingly unlikely that some of the more bullish solutions from yesterday evening will verify with regard to fog extent this morning. Have trimmed the Dense Fog Advisory to remove Lincoln County, with the remainder of zones maintained for the time being. That being said, trends will be watched closely over the next few hours and additional modifications to the Advisory may be needed.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Drier conditions are expected for today as a brief period of upper- level ridging develops behind Saturday's storm system. Despite the increased subsidence, a combination of morning fog, high clouds, and a Denver Cyclone will aid in keeping cooler temperatures in place across much of the forecast area. Those on the southern side of the cyclone may see temperatures in the mid to upper 40s thanks to downsloping effects off the Palmer Divide, whereas those on its northern extent should expect upper 30s to low 40s where northerly winds will keep cooler air sliding south. Patchy freezing fog is expected to begin developing over the eastern plains late tonight, with areas of dense fog likely setting in just before sunrise. Hi- res guidance continues to shift the corridor of thickest fog slightly with each run, but has continued to keep its southern most edge just making it into the airfield at DIA and northward along the I-25 corridor into Larimer County, as well as east along I-70 into Lincoln County. Anyone driving across the plains in the morning should be prepared to encounter patchy fog, with areas of significantly reduced visibilities to a quarter mile or less at times. Additionally, freezing fog can create slick surfaces which could lead to slippery driving conditions on top of lowered visibilities. A Dense Fog Advisory has been issued for Washington County from 1AM to 10AM, and for the northern I-25 Corridor and adjacent plains from Denver northward, areas along Highway 34, and I- 70 east of Denver from 4AM to 10AM. Conditions should start to improve by late morning.

Synoptically, things look in decent agreement across ensemble suites and deterministic outputs alike, with regards to the next approaching shortwave expected to move across the Rockies on Monday. For Colorado, it looks like the axis of the upper-level ridge will push east by Monday morning, leaving southwesterly flow aloft in its wake. Afternoon high temps are forecast to remain five to ten degrees below normal across the lower elevations, with our northern mountain valleys staying right around seasonal values. Cross sections show a deepening moisture profile throughout the day, with snow showers likely developing in the mountains by the afternoon. Moisture still looks unimpressive with this next wave, but despite our lower elevations remaining dry, we should at least see some light mountain snowfall accumulations overnight into Tuesday morning (generally two inches or less), with low chances for some very light accumulations for portions of the Palmer Divide.

Upper-level ridging will rebuild across the Rockies behind Monday's disturbance. Afternoon temperatures will gradually warm each day through the week, with mild and dry conditions looking likely for Thursday's holiday celebrations. There are enough uncertainties with the the evolution of our next potential storm system to not completely rule out light mountain snow showers through the week, but our lower elevations are on track to remain dry through the forecast period.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: The gradual warming trend will continue Thanksgiving Day through the weekend. A weak vort-max will pass through around Wednesday night/Thursday, but nearly all ensemble members are now dry for this event, and it will largely just slow the warming trend.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Patchy dense freezing fog persists over portions of the High Plains Sunday morning.
- Chilly temperatures will continue through Tuesday.
- Marginally high winds will be possible Tuesday night for the wind prone areas of southeast Wyoming.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Snow shower activity has dissipated across the area early this morning as the upper level low responsible for yesterday's unsettled weather moves off to the east. A weak surface high pressure system has settled in over the High Plains this morning, but the pressure differential across the area is fairly small. Thus, surface winds are mostly light but somewhat disorganized over the High Plains, while breezy westerlies continue in the I-80 wind prone areas on the other side of the subtle boundary. GOES satellite imagery in the nighttime microphysics RGB indicates a spotty region of low-clouds expanding over portions of the High Plains this morning, supported by very light upslope flow as the surface high. Where this intersects the terrain, we are seeing some patchy visibility reductions. Temperatures are well below freezing, so there may be some light riming on elevated surfaces. In addition, due to the disorganized forcing from the surface high pressure system, fog will probably not be very consistent and may roll in and out multiple times. Due to that, opted for a Special Weather Statement which continues over Laramie, Banner, and Kimball counties until 9AM. We do have some fog showing up further north too, but it is more isolated outside of the southern counties.

Chilly temperatures will prevail today. Most locations will end up between the mid 30s and lower 40s as mid to high level cloud cover increases from the west. While portions of Carbon and Albany counties will start off breezy today, expect winds to be on a general decreasing trend with light winds by tonight. Surface pressure will continue to increase to our northeast overnight, turning winds to the southeast over most of the High Plains. This airmass isn't exactly moist, but it will contain enough moisture to develop a few areas of patchy fog again towards Monday morning. Exactly where is somewhat low confidence, so did not add fog into the official forecast yet. Despite weak ridging trying to build in tonight, most of the area will remain chilly Monday thanks to fairly widespread cloud cover. Highs should be generally close to what we see Sunday. Breezy conditions may be present in the morning in western Nebraska, but winds look generally light Monday as well. Another weak and disorganized split trough will approach the area Monday, but with weak forcing and unimpressive moisture, this looks most likely to just produce a few flurries in the mountains Monday night. PoPs are around 20-30% only for the higher mountains of the Snowy and Sierra Madre ranges, and less than 10% elsewhere.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Organized ridging will attempt to build back in over the area on Tuesday into Wednesday behind Monday's weak system. The split trough will mostly move out Tuesday morning, but the northern upper level low will be diving southward simultaneously. This will help drop surface pressure over northeast Wyoming or South Dakota, building the cross-barrier pressure gradient once again. Expect breezy westerlies to return to areas along and west of the Laramie Range Tuesday, and peak in strength Tuesday night with the maximum pressure gradient before the surface low begins to eject early Wednesday. Low-level height gradients are a little lower than usual thresholds for high winds per most model forecasts, but MSLP gradients are pretty strong. This should limit winds to just the gap wind areas. Current probabilities are around 60% for Arlington/Elk Mountain and 30% for Bordeaux and the I-80 summit. Tuesday's highs should be around 5F warmer than Monday with more sunshine returning, and then Wednesday's highs look similar, with the warming trend hampered by a reinforcing chilly airmass moving in behind the northern branch shortwave. Dewpoints will also be dropping during this period, so elevated fire weather conditions may return again, primarily in Albany, Laramie, and Platte counties.

The gradual warming trend will continue Thanksgiving Day through the weekend. A weak vort-max will pass through around Wednesday night/Thursday, but nearly all ensemble members are now dry for this event, and it will largely just slow the warming trend. Another round of stronger ridging will build into the west Friday into Saturday. the ridge will have a fairly potent jet streak aloft on its northeast flank corresponding to a temperature gradient. Exactly where this sets up will determine out weather outcome for Friday into Saturday. Ensembles are clustered into two scenarios. The first, made of of nearly all GEFS members and about 40% of ECMWF ensemble members includes a stronger, more amplified ridge that pushes the jet streak just to our northeast. This would lead to a significant warm-up Friday into the weekend. While conditions would still be breezy to windy, this scenario pushes the strongest gradients just far enough away to reduce the chance for high winds. In the other scenario, made up of the remaining 60% ECMWF ensemble members, the ridge is weaker and flatter, positioning the jet streak more or less directly over the area. This would lead to stronger winds (likely high winds), and the potential for respectable mountain snowfall. In addition, this scenario would mean cooler temperatures, and the potential for a stalled (weak) arctic front somewhere nearby. For now, the official forecast is closer to the first scenario, which has roughly a 60% chance of playing out, but elevated wind speeds and low PoPs for mountain snowfall are still included. For now, it looks fairly likely that Cheyenne will add at least a week to the snow-less streak after surpassing the record latest first measurable snowfall of the season on Friday.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: By Tuesday morning, the trough will move east of our area, and ridging builds in. Conditions through Wednesday are expected to be dry with temperatures remaining near or slightly below normal.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Generally dry and cooler conditions return for Sunday.
- A quick moving system will bring areas of rain and snow showers for Monday.
- Active weather remains possible for Thanksgiving week, but some details still remain uncertain. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Dry and cool weather is expected for Sunday with a weak ridge moving through the Intermountain West. Mid to high level clouds will move in from the west through the day as our next storm system approaches.

Moisture will begin to move into the area Sunday night as a weak low- amplitude trough moves through and brings southwesterly flow. This system will be fast moving with moisture and lift remaining limited. High-res models begin to develop light showers Monday morning over the Four Corners. This will bring a rain/snow mix for valley locations with mostly snow expected in the higher terrain above 6000 ft. There are some pockets of weak instability that may develop Monday afternoon (SBCAPE 50-100 J/kg) over southwest Colorado creating the possibility of locally heavier snowfall. The best chance for accumulating snow remains over the San Juans but accumulations are expected to be mostly light and be below advisory levels.
DRY AGAIN MIDWEEK, ACTIVE WEATHER POSSIBLE FOR END OF THE WEEK:

By Tuesday morning, the trough will move east of our area, and ridging builds in. Conditions through Wednesday are expected to be dry with temperatures remaining near or slightly below normal. The rest of the forecast period may remain active with some deterministic guidance showing another weak system for Thanksgiving Day. Northwesterly flow will primarily bring impacts to the Park Range, but exact details are uncertain at this time. Another system is possible next weekend, but ensemble members are still showing significant disagreement. Stay tuned on potential impacts to holiday travel plans.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: It will dry out again for Tuesday and much of Wednesday with below normal temperatures gradually warming towards mid week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry with continued below seasonal temperatures Sunday.
- Another quick moving system bringing light mountain snows and passing showers to the plains Monday into Monday night.
- Late week system still trending drier with better consensus on splitting flow with CO under the influence of a drier northern stream system around the Thanksgiving holiday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Broad shortwave ridging today over CO will transition to southwesterly flow aloft as the next upper trough takes shape across the western U.S. Today will be dry across all of southern CO with temperatures remaining below climo (mostly 40s plains and valleys with 20s and 30s mountains). Otherwise, high cloudiness will invade from the west and thicken through the day and winds remain relatively light. Winds will start to increase tonight as southwest flow aloft increases and the surface lee trough deepens in response. This will help keep min temperatures warmer than this mornings as enhanced westerly downslope flow kicks in. We could see some localized gusts up to 30 to 40 mph along the lower eastern slopes of the southeast mountains after midnight but this will serve to bump temperatures up into the 30s, instead of teens and 20s elsewhere.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Broad upper trough over the Great Basin will translate eastward across CO Monday and Monday night with snow spreading into the Continental Divide Monday morning, and across the valleys into the southeast mountains by afternoon. Isolated to scattered showers will spill off the mountains into the adjacent plains Monday night with the greatest coverage south of highway 50. Overall, system looks lacking for moisture, leading to only some light snow accumulations across the mountains, and a spotty trace to under an inch of snow across the plains. Timing of the upper trough passage at night across the plains will lead to lower snow levels and a better chance for lower elevation communities to at least see some snow flakes. However lacking much in the way of upslope and moisture, any snow amounts will be spotty and light with accumulations limited to cold surfaces. Not anticipating much in the way of travel impacts east of the I-25 corridor.

It will dry out again for Tuesday and much of Wednesday with below normal temperatures gradually warming towards mid week. Models are coming into better consensus with the next system for late week, with energy splitting as it dives to the south into Old Mexico. The northern stream trough, which still varies in amplitude and timing between the long range models and ensembles, moves across CO around Thanksgiving. Trend is still towards a drier and warmer forecast for much of the region late week into next weekend, though the central mountains could pick up some light snow accumulations with the passing system.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: Ensembles are in good agreement on building a stout ridge over the region from late Monday through at least Wednesday before any chance of weakening.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A cool and stable airmass will settle across the region through the weekend.
- A weak weather system will bring a chance of snow showers mainly to northern Utah Monday, with little accumulation.
- Another weak system is forecast to cross the region on Thanksgiving. This will bring a small chance for valley rain and mountain snow to northern Utah, while southern Utah remains largely dry.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Cool and stable conditions have built into the region today as we find ourselves under the influence of a weak upper level ridge in the wake of a cold trough. Brief clearing that occurred across the region earlier this evening is now deteriorating as upper-level moisture tied to an approaching shortwave trough filters into the eastern Great Basin region. While we'll be under the influence of weak surface high pressure on Sunday, middle and high-level cloud cover will remain draped across the forecast area, helping to keep surface temperatures cooler.

A weakening trough moving in from the eastern Pacific will phase into Utah late sunday through Monday, though a majority of model solutions show a lack of moisture and strong dynamics that would support significant snowfall across Utah. As such, would anticipate light snowfall across the northern Utah mountains and lee side valley areas on Sunday night through Monday, with minor accumulations at best. It's worth noting that there remains a small cohort of models that favor much more robust dynamics that would favor higher intensity precipitation, not only for northern Utah but also for a portion of central and southern Utah. Even then, total SWE associated with these more robust solutions favors only around 0.1" or less in the terrain... with around a 10% chance or less of occurrence.

Ensembles are in good agreement on building a stout ridge over the region from late Monday through at least Wednesday before any chance of weakening. Upstream energy over the eastern Pacific region may act to supply a series of weak impulses through the large scale ridge that should (hopefully) act to limit the potential for persistent valley inversions... but that's about it. Would anticipate any energy moving through the broad ridge to serve up light snowfall in the high terrain, but not much else. The next big storm cycle will have to wait until we see a breakdown of this ridge.

2660.travel_advice: Dangerous avalanche conditions. Careful snowpack evaluation, cautious route-finding and conservative decision-making essential.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: You can trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you from a distance, from below, or on steep, shady leeward slopes. Strong winds formed thicker and stiffer slabs below ridgelines and around convexities in the alpine, burying a layer of weak snow. The most dangerous slopes are north and northeast-facing slopes above treeline.
Avoid leeward, drifted slopes steeper than around 35 degrees to avoid triggering a dangerous avalanche. Safer travel can be found on lower-angled slopes and in wind-sheltered areas below treeline.

2753.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Dylan Craaybeek
bottom_line: You can trigger an avalanche on some steep slopes that face west through north to east near and above treeline. Most of these avalanches will be small, but on a wind-loaded terrain feature, they could grow large enough to bury you. You can also trigger these avalanches from a distance, so be aware of steep slopes overhead and other parties nearby. If you experience obvious signs of instability, such as shooting cracks or collapsing in the snow as you travel across it, this is a sign that you found a dangerous area and should avoid traveling on or directly under steep slopes.

2754.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Most slopes are generally safe from avalanches due to shallow or discontinuous snow cover. You might be able to trigger a small avalanche if you find stiff, wind-drifted snow below ridgelines, on lee slopes, and around rocky outcrops in the alpine.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: There isn't enough snow for avalanches on most slopes. Steer around hard drifts of snow on steep terrain features and below ridgetop in the alpine.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are still thin and lack a slab, so avalanche danger is LOW. You should be able to steer around isolated pockets of firmer wind-drifted snow, especially in steep terrain.
